title: Mendel's peas
hookLine: an Augustinian friar in a monastery garden discovers the laws of heredity

lines: A STRIP OF GARDEN BEHIND THE ABBEY.
cards: Behind the walls of an abbey in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic, there's a narrow strip of garden.

A friar in a dark habit kneels in it with a small brush, moving pollen from one pea flower to another by hand, then tying a little bag over the flower so no bee can undo his work. He writes everything down.
Tall plants, short plants. Smooth peas, wrinkled peas. Yellow, green.
Season after season, he plants, crosses, counts and records. His brothers sing the hours in the chapel, and he walks back out to the rows. His name is Gregor Mendel.

teach.h: AN AUGUSTINIAN FRIAR IN THE GARDEN.
teach.b: Mendel was an Augustinian friar, in a religious order that lives by a rule of prayer and shared life. His abbey valued learning, and sent him to study science.

What he found in the garden: traits from the parent plants don't simply blend together like paint. Cross a tall pea with a short one, and the next generation can all come up tall. The shortness seems gone.

But let those tall plants pollinate themselves, and in the next generation short ones come back. Something was being carried, hidden and passed on, in units that kept their identity from one generation to the next.
Those units are now called genes, and their study genetics. Mendel had neither word. He had peas, patience and a notebook.
His results drew little notice. He became abbot, busy running the house, and died before the world caught up. Later scientists found his paper and saw he had already worked it out in a garden.

The Bible's first chapter has an old line about what he was watching, in the King James translation: "the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind." Like gives rise to like.
Genesis names the pattern; the friar counted how it works, row by row.
Paul borrowed a gardener's picture too, writing about the church at Corinth: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." The planter and the waterer do their part, and wait.
Mendel's whole method was that kind of waiting.

how: Some religious orders, the Augustinians among them, keep gardens, schools and libraries alongside their life of prayer, and some of their members have worked as scientists.

games.why: Mendel bred from those tall plants, letting them pollinate themselves, and short plants came back. the trait had been hidden, not lost.

practice: If there's a plant near you, touch the soil and give it what it needs, water or light; if not, hold a seed or picture one in your palm, and think of everything packed into that small thing, waiting.
You don't make it grow; you give it what it needs and wait. If you pray, say Paul's line, I have planted, but God gave the increase; if not, stay with the patience of it.

wordCard.voice: Mendel's peas. The garden experiments of Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, which showed that traits are passed on in units that can hide and return.
